title: How I teach: the inverse square law (rate of photosynthesis) at KS4 ynthesis-at-ks4/
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino describes how she rebuilt her teaching of the inverse square law in KS4 photosynthesis after being caught out by a worksheet question she could not answer herself. Her earlier approach, giving the equation and a couple of practice questions, was too rushed to be useful. She now lists the questions students must be able to answer, retrieves prerequisite knowledge through a low-stakes quiz, and builds the idea from a torch demonstration to a drawn diagram showing light spread over one, four and nine squares. A table, a student-written summary and only then the equation follow, with recall and homework in the next lesson. The piece is a worked example of sequencing, cognitive-load management and teacher planning.
points: Planning a lesson by first listing the exact questions students should be able to answer keeps the explanation focused.
A low-stakes retrieval quiz on prerequisites at the start reduces cognitive load for the new idea.
Moving from a physical demonstration to a drawn diagram, a table, a written summary and finally the equation lets students see why the law holds before they apply it.
Working the problems yourself before setting them avoids the failure that prompted the change.
quotes: Then one day, I made the mistake of giving my top set a worksheet I hadn’t previously attempted myself. A question on the inverse square law confused the class and they asked for help. And I couldn’t work it out either. Obviously, after the lesson, I asked for help, understood the question and explained it in the following lesson. I could have avoided this embarrassment if I had planned my lesson better.

I also came to realise that my rushed explanation was not sufficient and that I needed to spend some time thinking about how I introduce the equation linking light intensity and the distance from a light source.

The questions in italics are ones that I cover before discussing the inverse square law and so I will not discuss them in this post. I reduce the cognitive load in this lesson by ensuring pre-requisite knowledge is retrieved at the start in the form of a low stakes quiz.

I use a torch under the visualiser to demonstrate that when I move the torch away from the page on my visualiser book, the brightness decreases, and the reverse is true when I bring the torch closer to the page.

The pattern on the second piece of paper shows how the light falls on a greater area that is twice as high and twice as wide. This means that the light intensity is spread over four boxes instead of one. In other words, light intensity is a quarter of the intensity hitting the first piece of paper.

In the following lesson, I check that the different factors and their effects on the rate of photosynthesis can be recalled. I also give a few questions on the inverse square law for homework as well to ensure it is part of the students’ independent practice.
